title: When Federal Law Overrides the States
hook: Who decides what warning goes on a bottle of weed killer — a state jury or the federal government? The answer turns on a quiet but powerful rule called preemption.
key_points: Under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, valid federal law overrides conflicting state law.
When Congress regulates an area thoroughly, it can 'preempt' — displace — state-law claims in that field.
In a 2026 case over Roundup weed killer, the Supreme Court sided with maker Monsanto on this question.
The dispute: whether a federal pesticide-labeling regime overrides state lawsuits demanding extra warnings.
Preemption is a core federalism tool — it decides which level of government has the final say.
content_html: Most fights between government and citizen are about what the rules should be. A quieter, more structural fight is about who gets to make them — the national government or the states. That is the question of preemption, and in June 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court answered a high-profile version of it.
extra_html: The case grew out of lawsuits over Roundup, the popular weed killer. NPR's Carrie Johnson reports that the central issue was who decides what warnings must appear on a pesticide label — and whether a federal labeling regime overrides state-law claims arguing the label should have warned of cancer risk. The Court sided with the manufacturer, Monsanto. The durable idea underneath the headline is the doctrine of preemption. The Constitution's Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law the "supreme law of the land," so where state and federal law genuinely conflict — or where Congress has regulated a field so completely that it leaves no room for additional state requirements — the federal rule wins and the state claim is displaced. Preemption is one of federalism's sharpest instruments: it doesn't decide whether a warning is wise, only which level of government holds the final say. (This card describes U.S. constitutional law specifically; other federations resolve national-versus-regional conflicts in their own ways.)

flashcards.prompt: What is 'preemption' in a federal system?
flashcards.back_html: The rule that valid federal law overrides conflicting state law. When Congress regulates a field thoroughly, it can displace state-law claims in it.

flashcards.prompt: Which constitutional principle makes federal preemption possible?

choices.text: The Supremacy Clause, which makes valid federal law override conflicting state law
The right to a jury trial in civil cases
The separation of the legislative and executive branches

flashcards.explanation_html: Preemption flows from the Supremacy Clause: where federal and state law conflict in an area Congress has occupied, the federal rule prevails.

flashcards.prompt: What was the central question in the 2026 Roundup case the Court decided for Monsanto?

choices.text: Whether a federal pesticide-labeling regime overrides state suits demanding extra warnings
Whether states may regulate farming at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Per NPR, the issue was who decides label content — and whether federal law displaces state failure-to-warn claims. That is a preemption question.
